_about: Say nothing twice. Krish, 2026-10-17: "Asa, everything I say to you, whether it's feedback or ideas, you should always be thinking about why I'm saying it and what that means for the future. I want a \"say nothing twice\" policy in this engine, where you understand me, how we work, and how we iterate." Every piece of feedback or idea he gives becomes one entry: his exact words (an excerpt, never a transcript), why he said it, what it means from now on, and where it is now enforced, each place with a marker that must stay there. scripts/check_failures.py (run first in every session) fails when a marker is gone, and lists the learnings still open. A failure he raised goes in config/failures.json; everything else he says goes here.

learnings.krish: the fact that I need to approve/sign off on titles and headers and thumbnail headings and whatnot after recording is an important distinction because only after recording do I really feel like I've got a message. Usually I change or understand a fair bit more after reading a script out loud than I do creating a script.
learnings.why: Reading the script aloud is where he finds his message, and he ad-libs a third of it (narration ledger). Packaging written before the take is written for a message he has not landed yet, so it gets redone.
learnings.means: No title, headline, thumbnail word, card heading or chapter divider is put to him or drawn before a take is on the record; after it, the options come from what he said on camera and his playbook, all at once.

learnings.krish: This isn't a well-known concept and it's not a well-known media business. ... Why can't you understand why I absolutely hate, detest, loathe these? They're offensive to me. They hurt my soul.
learnings.why: His purpose is to make what is coming legible to people; a line only legible to someone who has already watched the video is the opposite of it, and a cheap, cryptic one costs the credibility a new brand for senior people depends on. It also proved lessons already on file were ignored: the surface formula ("under 4 words", "a curiosity gap") was followed over his principle.
learnings.means: Every line a stranger sees first names a real thing in plain words and says something true about it; his principles outrank any formula; nothing reaches him before a cold reader with no context can explain it; fewer, better options, never a pile.

learnings.krish: These headings are so stupid it's insane. I can't believe you're putting these to me. Then: "I do worry that using my own words for headings and chapter names will lose some of what makes this feel like a real media channel"
learnings.why: First they were written to pass the title checker (names stuffed in, label strings, bare numbers), not to be read in a second. The fix overcorrected into pasting his transcript, which loses the edited layer that makes a channel feel professional.
learnings.means: Headings and chapter dividers are an editorial layer in one channel style: one device across the episode, each line a short claim or promise naming the real thing, a kicker with the source and date, built on what he says at that moment and his best phrases, never pasted from the transcript and never written to pass the checker.

learnings.krish: do you not want to get sign off on headings and titles first so you can punch through to 100% without me?
learnings.why: His decisions are the only part of production that needs him. Asked mid-run, or queued behind slow machine work (screen captures, renders), they keep him on call for hours and the piece waits on him at the end instead of the start. He wants to answer once and then not be needed.
learnings.means: Once a take is on the record, the first thing a session does is put ONE sign-off sheet to him with every decision that is his for the piece (titles, cover and thumbnail words, title card, headings and chapter dividers, the intro stand-off, any script or speed choice), before any machine step that waits on it; then it finishes to publish-ready without coming back, except for a send, publish, spend or delete.

learnings.krish: These are still awful. I'm getting exhausted. The story is about there being so many recent AI model releases and figuring out if that's actually important, why it's speeding up, and what choices a user is going to have to make (or what gears are going to be hidden from them in the future). It's a "mind the gap" piece remember. Why do I have to remind you about what this story is about?
learnings.why: He judges a line first by whether it tells the piece's story; each round I fixed the last complaint and lost the story, so he had to restate it and is exhausted by it.
learnings.means: When he states what a piece is about, his words go in the plan's story.md and every later line (titles, cover, thumbnail, title card, chapters, headings, channel copy) is judged against them first; without a statement, the outline's spine and the series' question.

learnings.krish: in general ensure nothing is ever not accessible by another session, ever
learnings.why: A handover lost work because captures, renders and transcripts lived only in one cloud container; the next session, often on his other account, would have had to remake them.
learnings.means: Before a session stops, everything it made or used that another session may need is either committed (code, configs, specs, transcripts, small data) or sent to the post's library folder with send.py (screenshots, renders, panels, exhibits), and the handover names where each is. Nothing lives only in .cache or a workflow journal.

learnings.krish: They should all become standing rules.
learnings.why: One six-day session used about half of a 20x Max plan in a week: every step re-read a context that sat at a median of 459k tokens; and four paid fact-check reruns cost about four times the estimate.
learnings.means: One fresh session per job, handover between topics, few big steps, no big outputs in the chat, Sonnet for production work, agents only where a separate reader is needed, and paid runs estimated from the meter.

learnings.krish: I don't need these as artefacts. I need them as Markdown. This is a good example of why you waste tokens. The only artefacts I need are the two published boards being fully up to date.
learnings.why: A request for three Markdown files was also built onto both boards, costing a board read, a rebuild and two publishes he did not ask for.
learnings.means: Files he asks for are handed over as files. Artifacts are only the week's publish boards, kept up to date.

learnings.krish: yes, if you are 110% sure this does not degrade the quality of the output - this cannot happen.
learnings.why: He wants the engine cheaper to run (half a 20x Max plan in one week, $45.51 of API in seven days), but a saving that makes the work worse is not a saving to him.
learnings.means: Every cost change is one of three kinds: the same input read fewer times (caching, carry-forward, fresh sessions, a shorter start), mechanical work on a cheaper model held by deterministic checks, or a refusal before a paid run or a giant read. Fewer judges, smaller source sets, lower effort on writing or anything else that changes what the model reads for a decision is out. A cost change is measured first: one that the meter shows saves nothing is not made.
